title: The Journalistic Ethic
description: Objectivity, fairness, accuracy, accountability — the working creed of the press

concepts.title: What Journalism Is For
concepts.contentHtml:
Journalism is older than its formal ethics. The penny press of the 1830s, the wire agencies of the 1850s, the muckrakers of the 1900s, and the tabloid press of the 1920s all preceded any codified professional norms. The recognisable modern journalistic ethic coalesced in the early 20th century, alongside the first journalism schools (Columbia's, founded 1912 by an endowment from Joseph Pulitzer) and the first industry codes (the American Society of News Editors' "Canons of Journalism," 1923).

The most influential modern statement is Bill Kovach and Tom Rosenstiel's The Elements of Journalism (2001), which lists ten principles. The first is the most important: journalism's first obligation is to the truth. The second locates the journalist's loyalty with citizens, not with employers, advertisers, or sources. From those two follow the working norms: verify rigorously, maintain independence from those you cover, monitor power, provide a forum for public criticism, keep significant news significant, make news comprehensive and proportional.

None of this is law. In most democracies, the press is bound only by general laws (defamation, copyright, contempt of court) and, for broadcasters, lighter regulatory codes. The rest is professional convention, enforced through training, peer pressure, and the cost of a damaged reputation. That makes journalistic ethics fragile in the way a working scientific community is fragile: it depends on people who care about the work doing it carefully.

concepts.title: Accuracy, Verification, and the Two-Source Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The most basic professional virtue is accuracy. A reporter who gets the basic facts wrong — names misspelled, dates off, quotes mangled — has no claim on the reader's attention regardless of how good the prose is. Accuracy is a habit, not a disposition: it is built by checklists, fact-checks, and the practice of verification.

The single best-known rule of newsroom verification is the two-source rule: do not publish a contested factual claim on the basis of a single source. Independent corroboration — a second person, a document, a video, a contemporaneous record — is what separates news from rumour. The rule is associated with Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein's Washington Post reporting on Watergate (1972–1974), where editor Ben Bradlee insisted on it ruthlessly. The rule is not magic — two collaborating sources can be wrong together — but it is the load-bearing convention.

Verification has had to expand for new evidence types. Open-source intelligence (OSINT) groups like Bellingcat have shown how social-media images, flight-tracking data, satellite imagery, and metadata can be cross-referenced to corroborate or refute claims. The verification toolkit has grown; the underlying ethic has not changed.

concepts.title: Objectivity, Independence, Accountability
concepts.contentHtml:
The most contested professional norm is objectivity. The strong sense — that journalists can describe the world from no point of view at all — is incoherent and indefensible; no scholar of journalism takes it seriously. The working sense is more modest: a discipline of checking one's own assumptions, presenting evidence rather than opinion, giving relevant parties a fair hearing, and distinguishing reporting from commentary. Kovach and Rosenstiel call this "discipline of verification" and warn against confusing it with neutrality between truth and falsehood.

Independence is the closely related principle that journalists should not be financially or politically beholden to those they cover. The classical tools are firewalls between newsroom and advertising, conflict-of-interest disclosure, and bans on accepting gifts or paid speeches from sources. The platform era has eroded some of these — paid posts, sponsored content, and personal-brand reporters complicate the picture — but the norm remains.

Accountability closes the loop. Journalists are powerful. The professional response to that power is to correct errors visibly, name the reporter and editor responsible for a story, publish ombudsman or reader-editor columns, and submit to outside scrutiny — press councils, libel courts, and the judgment of one's own readers. A journalism that refuses correction is not a journalism worth defending.

title: Reporting: The Five Ws & Story Structure
description: Inverted pyramid, lede, nut graf — how a news story is built

concepts.title: The Five Ws and the Lede
concepts.contentHtml:
The reporter's first job is to know what the story is. The traditional checklist is the Five Ws (and an H): who, what, when, where, why, and how. Before writing a sentence, a reporter should be able to answer those six questions cleanly. If they can't, they are not yet ready to write.

The opening sentence — the lede (deliberately misspelled in newsroom slang to avoid confusion with the metal that holds type) — should usually pack the most newsworthy of those answers into 25–35 words. The classic "hard-news lede" might read: "A 6.4-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of southern Honshu early Tuesday, killing at least 12 people and triggering tsunami warnings as far south as Taiwan." Compact, factual, front-loaded.

Other story types take other ledes. Feature ledes open with a scene or character to draw the reader in before stating the news. Anecdotal ledes begin with a small concrete story that illustrates a larger trend. The choice depends on the kind of story, but the underlying discipline is the same: the first sentence is real estate, and the reader will not stay long unless it pays.

concepts.title: The Inverted Pyramid
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant structure of a news story is the inverted pyramid: most important information at the top, supporting detail in descending order of importance underneath. The reader who quits after the first paragraph still gets the gist; the reader who quits after the third paragraph gets more. Background, history, and quotes from less central voices are pushed toward the bottom.

The form has several origins. The telegraph billed by the word and could fail mid-message; reporters learned to lead with the essential. Editors trimming for column-inches preferred stories that lost their tail without losing their meaning. Readers, then as now, scan rather than read. The pyramid suits all three constituencies.

The pyramid is not the only structure, and over-reliance on it produces dull, repetitive stories. Long-form, investigative, and feature pieces use narrative structures — chronological, scenic, looping — that can hold a reader for thousands of words. But for daily news, the pyramid remains the default, and a young reporter who can write a clean inverted-pyramid story has acquired a real and portable craft.

concepts.title: The Nut Graf and Story Architecture
concepts.contentHtml:
Between the lede and the body sits the nut graf (or "nut paragraph") — the paragraph that tells the reader, explicitly, why the story matters and what they are about to learn. In a hard-news pyramid the nut may be implicit in the lede; in a feature it is essential. A useful test: if you cut the nut graf, can the reader still tell what the story is about? If yes, the nut isn't pulling its weight; if no, it is doing its job.

Beyond lede and nut, a well-built story has visible architecture: clear sections, transitions that move the reader forward without summarising backward, sourced specifics rather than vague claims ("a 23% increase" rather than "significant growth"), and a kicker — a final paragraph or quote that gives the reader something to take away. Veteran editors talk about a story's "load-bearing facts": the small handful of details on which the rest depends. Reporters lose readers when they bury or muddle those facts; they keep readers when each paragraph earns its place.

None of this is a formula. The form is a scaffolding the reporter inhabits and, when the story warrants, breaks out of. But a writer who has not first mastered the standard structures rarely succeeds at breaking them.

title: Beats, Sources, Verification
description: Cultivating sources, on-the-record vs background, the two-source rule

concepts.title: The Beat System
concepts.contentHtml:
Most full-time reporters work a beat: a defined area of coverage — courts, City Hall, the Pentagon, the central bank, a particular industry, a neighbourhood, a sport. The beat structure is so universal in newsrooms that it is easy to forget it is a choice, with consequences.

Beats produce expertise. A reporter who has covered the FDA for five years knows the agency's recent decisions, its key staff, and its institutional history. They can read a press release and immediately tell whether it is news, spin, or an attempt to bury something. That accumulated knowledge is the main asset a beat reporter brings to a story; a parachuted-in generalist often cannot match it.

Beats also produce capture risk. A reporter who covers the same officials for years grows close to them and may come to share their assumptions. Newsrooms manage this with rotation, with skeptical editors, and with formal independence rules. The good beat reporter has both deep relationships and the willingness to write stories that burn them when the story warrants. That is harder than it sounds.

concepts.title: Source Categories: On the Record, Background, Off the Record
concepts.contentHtml:
Every conversation with a source happens under terms — sometimes negotiated, sometimes assumed. The standard categories, with minor variation between newsrooms, are:

  • On the record: anything the source says can be quoted with attribution by name and title. Default unless otherwise stated.
  • On background: information can be used and quoted, but not attributed by name ("a senior State Department official said").
  • On deep background: information can be used to inform reporting but not directly quoted at all.
  • Off the record: information cannot be used, though it may help the reporter find an on-the-record source for the same material.

These rules are conventions, not contracts. They are also routinely abused — by sources who try to retroactively reclassify damaging quotes, and by reporters who push the line. The professional rule is that the terms must be agreed before the relevant information is shared, not after; a source cannot say something on the record and then declare it off the record once they regret it.

Senior reporters generally try to keep as much as possible on the record and use background sparingly, on the principle that anonymous sourcing weakens stories. Anonymous sources are sometimes necessary — for whistleblowers facing retaliation, for vulnerable people, for officials whose jobs depend on discretion — but the burden is on the reporter to justify their use.

concepts.title: Verification: Standards and Failures
concepts.contentHtml:
Verification is the discipline that turns information into journalism. The classical practices are familiar: the two-source rule for contested factual claims; document-first reporting where the document exists; back-checks to the people quoted to confirm their words and titles; and fact-checking the finished piece, often by a separate team in the most rigorous magazines.

Verification is also where journalism's most public failures happen. Stephen Glass at The New Republic (1995–1998) and Jayson Blair at The New York Times (1999–2003) fabricated stories over years before being caught. The Rolling Stone "A Rape on Campus" story (2014), which alleged a gang rape at the University of Virginia, was retracted after the reporter and editors had failed to interview key sources. These cases are studied in journalism schools precisely because they show how the discipline of verification can erode under deadline, ambition, or sympathetic identification with a source.

The digital era has added new verification problems. Social-media images can be staged, altered, or recycled from earlier events. Deepfaked video and AI-generated voice make synthetic evidence cheap. Tools — reverse-image search, geolocation, metadata extraction, content-authenticity standards — help, but they shift the verification problem rather than solve it. The principle remains: do not publish what you have not verified.

title: Investigative Journalism
description: Watergate to Panama Papers — long-form accountability reporting

concepts.title: What Investigative Journalism Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Investigative journalism is the systematic uncovering of facts that someone — usually someone powerful — has tried to keep hidden. It is the most expensive, slowest, and legally riskiest form of journalism, and the one most often invoked to justify the rest of the press's privileges.

The category overlaps with daily reporting but is recognisably distinct. Investigative pieces typically take weeks to years rather than hours; they involve multiple sources often built over time; they rely on documents — leaked, FOIA'd, or court-obtained — as much as on interviews; and they pursue stories that the subjects do not want told. The American Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting was established in 1953; ICIJ (the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists) has organised cross-border collaborations like the Panama and Pandora Papers.

The justification offered by the profession is straightforward: where institutions police themselves, scandals fester. Watchdog journalism is the working press's argument for democratic indispensability. Whether that argument fully cashes out in any given case is another question, but the framing is universal across democratic newsrooms.

concepts.title: Watergate: The Template
concepts.contentHtml:
The defining case of post-war investigative journalism is the Washington Post's coverage of the Watergate scandal. On June 17, 1972, five burglars were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate complex. Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, then in their late twenties, traced the burglary up the chain of command — eventually to senior White House staff and President Richard Nixon himself — across two years of reporting.

The reporting was made possible by, among other things: editor Ben Bradlee's insistence on the two-source rule; publisher Katharine Graham's willingness to back the paper through enormous legal and political pressure; a single high-level confidential source inside the FBI (revealed only in 2005 to have been Associate Director Mark Felt, codenamed "Deep Throat"); and patient documentary work tracing campaign finance through bank records.

Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974. The episode became the lasting template for adversarial investigative journalism in democracies — and the ambition that journalism schools and recruiters have invoked ever since. It is also the template for what investigative reporting actually requires: time, money, institutional backbone, and patient verification.

concepts.title: The Cross-Border Era: Snowden, Panama, and Collaborative Journalism
concepts.contentHtml:
The 21st century has reshaped investigative journalism around large leaks and cross-border collaboration. The 2010 release of US diplomatic cables to WikiLeaks, partnered with The Guardian, Der Spiegel, The New York Times, and others, established a new model: a single archive, multiple newsrooms, coordinated publication. The 2013 disclosures of US and UK mass-surveillance programmes by Edward Snowden, reported by Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras, and Barton Gellman, took the same form.

The Panama Papers (2016, 11.5 million documents from the law firm Mossack Fonseca) and Pandora Papers (2021, 11.9 million documents on offshore wealth) extended the model to financial disclosure, with hundreds of journalists at ICIJ partner organisations working in parallel for months under embargo. The investigations brought down a sitting prime minister (Iceland's Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson), forced policy changes, and produced criminal cases — at the cost of one murdered Maltese journalist, Daphne Caruana Galizia, killed by a car bomb in 2017 while reporting on the same offshore networks.

The risks are not abstract. Investigative reporters are jailed, sued into bankruptcy, and killed for their work. The Committee to Protect Journalists records dozens of journalists murdered each year in connection with their reporting. Watchdog journalism is one of the press's strongest arguments for itself — and one of its costliest.

title: Photojournalism & Documentary
description: Capa to Salgado — image as evidence, witness, and argument

concepts.title: The Birth of Photojournalism
concepts.contentHtml:
News photography became practical in the 1880s with the halftone process, which translated photographs into the dot patterns a printing press could reproduce. Before halftone, illustrated newspapers used wood engravings copied from photographs by hand; the photograph itself stayed in the studio.

The first generation of photojournalists worked the new gap. Jacob Riis's How the Other Half Lives (1890) used flash photography of New York tenements to put what readers had only read about into a form they could not look away from. Lewis Hine's images of children working in mines and mills, taken between 1908 and 1924 for the National Child Labor Committee, drove the campaigns that produced US child-labour law. Photographs were doing what journalism had always claimed to do — making distant suffering present — by means prose could not match.

The technological enabler of modern photojournalism was the small 35mm camera: the Leica (1925) and the Contax (1932) gave reporters a fast, portable, almost invisible tool that could shoot on the move in available light. The picture magazines — Vu in France (1928), Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung, and especially LIFE (US, 1936) and Picture Post (UK, 1938) — built genuinely visual journalism around this new instrument, often in the hands of central-European emigrés fleeing fascism.

concepts.title: Witness, Decisive Moment, Concerned Photography
concepts.contentHtml:
Three overlapping ideals run through 20th-century photojournalism.

Witness. Robert Capa, born Endre Friedmann in Budapest, photographed five wars between 1936 and 1954 — Spain, China, the Second World War, the 1948 Arab–Israeli conflict, and Indochina, where he was killed by a landmine. His best-known images, including the disputed Falling Soldier (1936) and the eleven surviving frames from D-Day's Omaha Beach (1944), shaped the public memory of those wars. Capa's working motto was: "If your pictures aren't good enough, you aren't close enough." The cost of being close enough is recorded in the long list of photojournalists killed on assignment.

Decisive moment. Henri Cartier-Bresson, Capa's friend and a co-founder with him of Magnum Photos in 1947, framed a different ideal in his book Images à la sauvette (1952, English title The Decisive Moment): photography as the recognition of a single fraction of a second when geometry, gesture, and meaning align. The discipline pushes photojournalism beyond the merely informative toward something with the formal weight of art.

Concerned photography. The Magnum tradition, extended by photographers like W. Eugene Smith, Sebastião Salgado, Susan Meiselas, and James Nachtwey, framed the photographer as an engaged moral witness — to famine in the Sahel, war in Central America, environmental catastrophe, mining and migration. The work openly takes a side. Whether that compromises objectivity, or simply makes its commitments visible, is one of the genre's permanent debates.

concepts.title: Documentary Film, Image Ethics, and the Digital Image
concepts.contentHtml:
Documentary cinema runs on parallel rails. John Grierson, a Scot, coined the term in a 1926 review and helped build British and Canadian documentary traditions. Frederick Wiseman's observational films of American institutions (Titicut Follies, 1967; Hospital, 1970) and Errol Morris's investigative reconstructions (The Thin Blue Line, 1988, which led to the release of a wrongly convicted man) extended what film could do as journalism. Streaming has produced a new wave: Citizenfour (Laura Poitras, 2014) on Snowden; Navalny (Daniel Roher, 2022); and a steady output from Frontline, Vice, and The New York Times's Visual Investigations team.

Image journalism has its own ethics — strict in the abstract, contested in practice. The basic rule is that news photographs should not be staged, composited, or substantively manipulated; cropping and tonal adjustment are allowed, anything that changes the content is not. Brian Walski at the Los Angeles Times was fired in 2003 for combining two Iraq-war frames into one. Tightly limited rules about altering crime-scene or subject identification have grown around concerns for victims and for ongoing legal cases.

The digital image stresses these norms. Smartphones make every bystander a potential photojournalist; AI generation makes synthetic photography cheap and convincing; misattribution and recontextualisation of real images is rampant on social media. The professional response has been a renewed emphasis on provenance — content-authenticity standards (the C2PA initiative), embedded metadata, and rigorous OSINT verification — and a recognition that the photograph's status as evidence, once nearly automatic, is something the profession now has to defend.

title: New Journalism & Long-form
description: Wolfe, Didion, Talese — literary technique applied to reporting

concepts.title: Long-form's Roots and the Magazine Form
concepts.contentHtml:
Reportage of book length and magazine length predates the inverted pyramid by a century. Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year (1722) is part history and part documentary fiction. James Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) is a reported biography that broke ground in observed scene and reconstructed dialogue. Charles Dickens's American Notes (1842) and George Orwell's The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and Homage to Catalonia (1938) are reported books in the modern sense.

The institutional home of long-form in the 20th century was the magazine. The New Yorker, founded in 1925 and reshaped under Harold Ross and William Shawn, built a model around extended reporting, light editorial framing, and the patience to let a story take 20,000 words. John Hersey's Hiroshima (1946) — a single August 31 issue of The New Yorker turned over entirely to the experiences of six survivors of the atomic bomb — became the canonical demonstration of what magazine journalism could do when it abandoned the pyramid altogether.

The magazine remained the engine of long-form through the postwar decades, with Esquire, Harper's, The Atlantic, and Britain's Sunday Times Magazine commissioning the work. Long-form has always been more expensive per word than daily reporting and more dependent on patrons — magazines, foundations, and now subscription platforms — than on advertisers alone.

concepts.title: The New Journalism: Wolfe, Didion, Talese, Capote
concepts.contentHtml:
The cluster of American writers who came to prominence in the 1960s — Tom Wolfe, Joan Didion, Gay Talese, Norman Mailer, Truman Capote, Hunter S. Thompson — practiced what Wolfe later christened the New Journalism. The argument, set out in Wolfe's anthology The New Journalism (1973), was that reporters could borrow the techniques of the realist novel — scene-by-scene construction, full dialogue, third-person interior point of view, status detail (the brand of car, the cut of the suit) — without sacrificing reportorial accuracy.

The signature works are familiar. Talese's "Frank Sinatra Has a Cold" (Esquire, 1966) reconstructed three months of unsuccessful interview attempts into a portrait of the singer's circle. Didion's Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968) used a quietly precise first-person voice to report Haight-Ashbury and California. Wolfe's The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test (1968) followed Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters in a third-person prose that absorbed their idiom. Capote's In Cold Blood (1966) — a reported account of the murder of a Kansas family — was marketed as a "non-fiction novel" and made the genre a publishing event.

The New Journalism was contested then and remains so. Critics argued the techniques invited fabrication or projection; defenders argued they made the reporting more honestly evident, with the writer's perspective on the page rather than hidden. Both lines of argument survive in current debates about long-form, narrative, and creative non-fiction.

concepts.title: Long-form Today: Podcasts, Newsletters, and the Subscription Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
The platform era nearly broke long-form journalism, then revived it. The 2000s saw classic long-form magazines shrink: Vanity Fair's feature counts dropped, regional Sunday magazines closed, alt-weeklies collapsed. The economics that had supported expensive reporting through advertising eroded as attention and ad dollars moved to platforms.

The 2010s and 2020s have produced unexpected new venues. Subscription publications — the New York Times Magazine, The Atlantic, The New Yorker, The Economist's 1843, Britain's Sunday Times "Insight" team — have funded long-form on the back of paying readers rather than advertisers. Substack and similar newsletter platforms have given individual reporters direct subscription relationships with readers; some long-form reporters now run one-person franchises that would have been institutionally impossible in 2005.

The fastest-growing long-form medium of the past decade is narrative podcasting. Serial (2014, the first season around the 1999 murder of Hae Min Lee) demonstrated that audio could carry reporting at audiobook length, and the format has multiplied: S-Town, The Daily, BBC Radio's investigative slots, the Ezra Klein Show. Long-form has not died; the venues, formats, and business models have multiplied. What survives is the underlying claim that some stories require thousands of words or hours of listening, and that journalism is the institution most willing to spend that effort.
